title: Supreme Court Rejects Missouri's New Congressional Map
summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court has again rejected a request from President Donald Trump's administration to use new congressional districts in Missouri that would favor Republicans. The order came Thursday with no noted dissents, clearing the way for the old map — passed by Republican legislators in 2022 — to be used in November's midterm elections.

Earlier in the week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee who handles emergency matters from Missouri, had already rejected a similar request without referring it to the full nine-member court. The high court's decision could influence which party controls the House of Representatives.

Missouri's redistricting battle has lasted more than a year. The new map was designed to help Republicans win seven of the state's eight House seats — a gain of one — by splitting a Kansas City-based district held by Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver into surrounding rural areas.

Opponents collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures to force a statewide vote on the new districts, submitting them in December. But Secretary of State Denny Hoskins waited until August — the same day as Missouri's primary — to reject the petition, arguing a referendum could not be used for congressional redistricting.

Last week, the Missouri Supreme Court ordered Hoskins to put the referendum on the November ballot, which he did. It also ruled the new districts never became law and were suspended back to December. The state appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, but Kavanaugh rejected the request.

On Thursday, a federal judge also allowed Missouri's top court to proceed with a contempt hearing against Hoskins for not following its orders. State attorneys had asked the judge to halt the hearing, but he declined. Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to enact new districts after Trump urged Republicans last year to redraw maps to their advantage.
why_it_matters: This case shows that even the rules for electing the people who make America's laws can be fought over in court, and whoever controls the House after November will shape decisions on taxes, schools and many other things teenagers live with every day.

background_read: Every ten years the United States carries out a census (an official count of everyone living in the country), and each state then redraws its congressional districts. Whichever party controls a state legislature usually draws those lines to help its own candidates win — a tactic known as gerrymandering, named after Elbridge Gerry, a nineteenth-century politician whose district was shaped like a salamander.

The U.S. Supreme Court (the country's highest court, which decides whether laws and official actions follow the Constitution) has ruled that federal judges cannot settle disputes about maps drawn purely to help one party, which is why fights like Missouri's often end up in state courts instead.

Missouri (a state in the middle of the country) has eight seats in the House of Representatives, and its constitution lets citizens collect signatures to force a public vote on a law they oppose. Texas (a large Republican-led state) was the first state to redraw its map after President Donald Trump urged Republicans to do so.

perspectives.description: They argue that state lawmakers elected by voters have the right to draw districts, and that a map reflecting Missouri's Republican-leaning electorate is fair. For them, the courts are interfering with decisions that belong to the state.

They say splitting a Kansas City district into surrounding rural areas dilutes the votes of city residents, who are more likely to be Democrats and Black voters. They see the courts' rulings as a check on a partisan power grab.

They note the U.S. Supreme Court has generally left partisan map-drawing to state courts and voters rather than federal judges. Missouri's fight is therefore a test of how far a state official can go in ignoring his own state's highest court.

The referendum may still appear on November's ballot, and the contempt case could set a precedent for whether election officials can pick which court orders to obey. Other states considering mid-decade redistricting will be watching the outcome closely.
